Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Apply the background knowledge of cemented and noncemented acetabular fixation in
primary total hip arthroplasty.
Determine the indications for cemented and noncemented acetabular fixation.
Demonstrate the surgical techniques for cemented and noncemented acetabular fixation.
Illustrate adjuvant screw placement for augmented acetabular fixation and associated
complications.
Primary Total Hip Arthroplasty
Overview


The ultimate goal of total hip arthroplasty (THA) is to restore normal hip biomechanics with
adequate sizing, position, and fixation of prosthetic components while minimizing
complications (Resource 1).
The ideal method to achieve optimal fixation of the acetabular component during primary THA
has been developed via training, evolution in surgical technique, and improvements in
component design and fixation.
Surgeons should be familiar with cemented and noncemented acetabular principles and
techniques.

Overview
Cemented acetabular components continue to play a role in clinical use; however, given
the excellent long-term results of noncemented cups with modern-generation liners (eg,
highly cross-linked polyethylene), the benefits of cemented fixation are less marked on
the acetabular side of the joint. Although cemented cups are indicated in specific
situations, evidence shows that, in many patients, a combination of cemented and
noncemented components, namely a hybrid THA implant (femoral and acetabular
components), may offer durable clinical results. Noncemented acetabular components
increased in popularity in the 1980s given their ease of insertion and consistent
osseointegration and the advantages of modularity. Long-term studies have since
described noncemented acetabular cups with survivorship greater than 90% and aseptic
loosening as an endpoint.1
Cemented Acetabular Fixation
Background
Cemented acetabular components are commonly used globally.
The use of cemented, all-polyethylene acetabular implants has declined drastically in the
United States since the introduction of noncemented components.

Background
SEND FEEDBACK

Although the use of cemented, all-polyethylene acetabular components (Resource 2) has
declined drastically in North America since the introduction of the noncemented
implants, cemented components continue to be commonly used globally. Most US
studies on cemented acetabular components have demonstrated excellent stability
during the first 10 years postoperatively, with high rates of radiographic loosening and
revision noted beyond 10 years postoperatively. To reduce failure rates from loosening,
cemented polyethylene components were augmented with metal backing in the early
1980s to reduce strain in the cement mantle; however, this design was universally
abandoned after early catastrophic failure. Although cemented acetabular implants are
associated with reduced costs, a more demanding surgical technique and the lack of
modularity are disadvantages to be considered with cemented, all-polyethylene
components.
Indications
Current indications for a cemented, all-polyethylene component primarily include elderly
patients in whom bone stock is thought to be inadequate to mechanically support a
noncemented acetabular component during the ingrowth process.
Patients with osteopenia or osteoporosis also are included in the relative indications for
cemented acetabular implants.

Indications
In a study of 2,000 primary Charnley arthroplasty implants (1,689 patients) followed for
25 years, patient age and length of follow-up most strongly correlated with outcomes.2
Survivorship free of revision for aseptic loosening was poorer for each subsequent
decade and varied from 68.2% in patients younger than 40 years to 100% in patients
older than 80 years.2 Males had a twofold higher rate of implant revision for aseptic
loosening than females (25-year survivorship was 95% for females and 81% for males; P
< 0.0001).2 Similar outcomes have subsequently been observed in larger registries and
meta-analyses, which explains the practice and recommendation that the ideal patients
for cemented cups are those older than 70 years.3 Similar to noncemented components,

recent evidence shows that longer-term results are substantially improved in all age
groups with the use of highly cross-linked polyethylene. Cemented cups also play a role
in complex primary THA and in the revision setting, in which they have been used
successfully in combination with impaction bone grafting or cementation into a well-
fixed noncemented cup, a highly porous cup with a damaged or no locking mechanism,
or a reconstruction cage. Cemented, dual-mobility acetabular components also are
viable options for complex primary THA in patients with bone deformity and in patients
with a higher risk of instability.
Cement Type
Evidence regarding differences in the outcomes with different cement types (antibiotic-
impregnated or plain) or with different levels of viscosity is inconclusive.
In contrast to total knee arthroplasty, evidence on the different viscosities of cement or
vacuum mixing in THA is limited.

Cement Type
Antibiotic-loaded bone cement is associated with a higher rate of revision in the first 6
months postoperatively and a lower rate of revision after 1.5 years postoperatively
compared with plain cement4 (Figure 1). The 2019 Australian Orthopaedic Association
National Joint Replacement Registry reported a 10% reduction in long-term revision rates
(follow-up, 10 years) with the use of antibiotic-loaded cement compared with plain
cement (5.7% versus 6.3%, respectively).5

Surgical Technique
The primary goal is to expose the underlying porous cancellous bone to maximize
interdigitation of cement to host bone.6
The acetabulum is reamed to the subchondral bone.
Manual hand pressure is used to encourage interdigitation, followed by an impactor to further
pressurize the cement.

Surgical Technique

Acetabular reaming generally is 2 to 4 mm greater than the diameter of the cup to be
inserted. A series of additional pilot holes can be made circumferentially around the rim
of the acetabulum, especially in any residual sclerotic areas, to enable better cement
intrusion and anchoring of the implant. The acetabulum is cleansed via pulsed lavage to
clear the interspaces of blood and fat, followed by the insertion of cement in the earlier
stages of hardening. Manual hand pressure is used to encourage interdigitation,
followed by the use of an impactor to further pressurize the cement. The interface is
carefully dried, and a component 2 to 4 mm smaller than the largest reamer used is
inserted. To ensure a uniform cement mantle that is 2 to 3 mm thick, cups with
polymethyl methacrylate studs on the surface can be used.
Learning Curve
More successful outcomes have been demonstrated as surgeons gains experience with
cementation technique, with a correlation reported between outcomes and surgeon frequency
of cementation.
The Australian Orthopedic Association National Joint Replacement Registry demonstrated
improvements in clinical results for surgeons who performed as few as 10 cemented
acetabular implants per year, with greater improvements observed after performing 25
procedures per year.7 Superior results have been reported in countries that use a high
proportion of cemented components compared with countries in which cemented prostheses
are used less frequently.8 Cemented components have an increasing role in certain patient
groups (eg, elderly patients, patients with osteopenia/osteoporosis, patients with metabolic
bone disease, immunocompromised patients in whom appropriate osseointegration and
ingrowth will be inhibited) despite the increasing use of noncemented components and
surgical technique.
Complications
The exothermic reaction that occurs during cement curing may injure soft-tissue structures
medial to the acetabulum, especially if the medial wall is thin.
Component loosening has been reported as a primary complication of cemented, all-
polyethylene acetabular components.

Progressive radiographic demarcation of the bone-cement interface is a strong risk factor for
component loosening.
Hodgkinson Criteria for Cemented Acetabular Components
In a series of 200 cemented, all-polyethylene Charnley sockets, a classification system was
developed that correlates the plain radiographic appearance of radiolucent lines at the bone-
cement interface in the DeLee and Charnley zones (I through III) with the following intraoperative
findings:9
No radiolucency: all solid
One zone radiolucency: 7% loose
Two zone radiolucency: 71% loose
Three zone (complete) radiolucency: 94% loose
Clear socket migration: 100% loose
In addition, if the radiolucent line is wider than 1 mm and if a radiolucency is present in two
or three zones, the socket is almost certainly loose (Resource 3).

Hodgkinson Criteria for Cemented Acetabular Components
Meta-analysis and registry studies have shown that cemented prostheses have a similar
or lower risk of revision compared with that of hybrid THA implants but demonstrated
poorer functional outcomes and patient quality of life scores.10 Although cemented
prostheses are lower in cost compared with hybrid and noncemented THA implants,
they may not be cost-effective given the higher complication and revision rates over
time.
Noncemented Acetabular Fixation
Basic Science
Osseointegration is the attachment of lamellar bone to metal implants without intervening
fibrous tissue.

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004019
7/20

Excessive micromotion inhibits noncemented component bony integration, which is based on
new bone ingrowth and ongrowth.
Initial fixation generally is obtained by press-fitting (with or without screw augmentation) a
slightly oversized component in the acetabulum.

Basic Science
Osseointegration is the attachment of lamellar bone to metal implants without
intervening fibrous tissue. In general, this occurs 4 to 12 weeks after component
implantation but may continue as long as 3 years postoperatively. Micromotion of more
than 150 μm leads to fibrous union, micromotion between 40 and 150 μm leads to a
combination of osseous and fibrous union, and micromotion of less than 20 μm
primarily renders cancellous bone formation and ingrowth. Excessive micromotion
inhibits noncemented component bony integration, which is based on new bone
ingrowth and ongrowth. Bone growing inside a porous surface is the ingrowth, and bone
growing onto a roughened surface is ongrowth, which is determined by implant surface
characteristics. Adequate bony contact and firm implant fixation are essential during
noncemented THA to minimize micromotion. The minimum bone coverage required for
stable acetabular fixation of contemporary, highly porous components ranges from 50%
to 60%11 (Resource 4). Initial fixation generally is obtained via press-fitting (with or
without screw augmentation) a slightly oversized component into the acetabulum.
Contraindications
Contraindications for noncemented implants are rare.
The two most common contraindications are severe osteoporosis that cannot mechanically
support a noncemented cup as ingrowth occurs and radiation necrosis of the pelvis.

Contraindications
In current practice, a modular, noncemented acetabular component is commonly used.
The two most common contraindications are severe osteoporosis that cannotSEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:51 PM
AAOS | Primary Total Hip Arthroplasty for Osteoarthritis: Acetabular Component
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004019
8/20

mechanically support a noncemented cup as ingrowth occurs and radiation necrosis of
the pelvis. Radiation necrosis of the pelvis can be recognized by a chalky-white
appearance of the reamed retroacetabular bone, indicating avascularity, in combination
with a patient’s clinical history. Cemented acetabular components may be an alternative
option for patients with a complex deformity; however, multi-hole shells or
reconstruction cages with multiple screws generally are used for immediate fixation and
stability.
Surface Coating
Most contemporary components have a porous titanium surface.
Given the high rates of successful osteointegration with these components, surface coatings,
such as hydroxyapatite, are rarely used because of their cost.

Surface Coating
Although several different noncemented designs were produced in the late 1980s and
early 1990s, most contemporary components have a porous titanium surface. Currently,
specialized coatings are primarily reserved for specialized components, such as
monoblock dual-mobility and resurfacing cups. In such cases, the ingrowth surface
consists of a cobalt-chromium alloy, which has been shown to be inferior to titanium as
an ingrowth surface, and the addition of hydroxyapatite may be important to ensure
that osteointegration occurs.
Surgical Technique
Adequate exposure is critical for noncemented acetabular reconstruction.
With most designs, 1 mm of under-reaming is appropriate; however, line-to-line reaming may
be acceptable.


Surgical Technique
The amount of under-reaming performed is based on surgeon preference, bone quality,
and particular implant design features. Factors that influence line-to-line reaming versus
under-reaming include:
Surface roughness
Implant stiffness
Differential between labeled and actual component diameter size
Integrity of host bone
With most designs, 1 mm of under-reaming is appropriate; however, line-to-line reaming
may be acceptable. Screws may be used for adjunct fixation.
Monoblock Components
Older generation designs stimulated debris from adjuvant screw micromotion.
Monoblock acetabular components were introduced to improve on earlier design
complications.
These components were more challenging to implant because the acetabular floor could not
be visualized through the screw holes during impaction.

Monoblock Components
The primary mode of failure for older generation acetabular component fixation was
osteolysis from particulate debris. Although polyethylene debris is primarily generated at
the bearing surface, wear also can occur secondarily at the backside interface between
the liner and cup. Monoblock acetabular components were introduced in the late 1990s
to improve on earlier design complications; however, these components were more
challenging to implant because the acetabular floor could not be visualized through the
screw holes during impaction. If revision was performed for acetabular wear or

instability, liner exchange was not possible. Cumulative 15-year survival rates of various
monoblock designs with loosening as an endpoint for revision have been excellent.
Massin Criteria for Noncemented Acetabular Component Migration
Definite loosening12 (Resource 5)
Acetabular migration of 2 mm or more in horizontal or vertical direction
Implant rotation
Screw breakage
Progressive bead shedding
Probable loosening
Radiolucent line larger than 1 mm at the implant-bone interface in all three zones without
migration, rotation, or screw breakage
Stable
Spot welds of streaming trabeculae and absence of the above findings
A randomized controlled trial reporting the 12-year results of 113 patients who received a
tantalum monoblock or a porous-coated titanium monoblock cup showed survivorship of
100% in the porous tantalum group.13
Contemporary Highly Porous Acetabular Designs
Porous metals are composed of a three-dimensional metal structure with interconnected
pores.
The increased porosity along the acetabular shell increases the amount of bone ingrowth, with
the goals of improved osseointegration and longevity.
Modern porous materials have transitioned from cobalt-chromium to titanium because
materials with greater flexibility and a lower modulus of elasticity have reduced the risk of
stress shielding while improving ingrowth properties.

Contemporary Highly Porous Acetabular Designs

Highly porous acetabular surfaces are rougher and are manufactured via a different
technology for improved initial press-fit and stability. The increased porosity along the
acetabular shell increases the amount of bone ingrowth, with the goal of improved
osseointegration and longevity. Modern porous materials have transitioned from cobalt-
chromium to titanium because materials with greater flexibility and a lower modulus of
elasticity have reduced the risk of stress shielding while improving ingrowth properties.
Several studies have reported 88% to 100% survivorship at 7- to 24.5-year follow-up14-22
(Table 1; Resource 6). Although highly porous metal acetabular components have
demonstrated excellent durability and clinical results in primary THA, the revision setting
represents the greatest opportunity for enhanced noncemented fixation surfaces to
have a substantial clinical effect in patients with bone loss and poor bone quality.

Adjuvant Acetabular Screw Fixation
Indications
Eccentric acetabular reaming that may jeopardize press fit
Poor bone quality, which may compromise initial mechanical fixation
Incomplete lateral coverage of the acetabulum (15% to 20%)
Medialization beyond the planned center of rotation of the joint

Indications
With the use of newer acetabular porous manufacturing designs, routine adjuvant screw
fixation is controversial. The use of highly cross-linked polyethylene has rendered
osteolysis from screw holes used as access pathways for particular debris a more
historical complication. As value-based care continues to emphasize decreasing
procedural costs, the routine use of adjuvant screws with newer cementless cup designs
may not be cost-effective; However, if concern exists with regard to the nitial mechanical
stability of a noncemented cup, adjuvant screws should be used. Screws provide
immediate mechanical stability that is critical for bone ingrowth. The screw holes allow
the surgeon to visualize the floor of the acetabulum, providing confirmation of full
component seating. Screw fixation can close any gaps created via incongruous

acetabular reaming. Adjuvant screw fixation may mitigate the loss of compressive
stresses and resulting shear stresses. Incomplete lateral coverage of the acetabulum
(15% to 20%) and medialization beyond the planned center of rotation of the hip also
may be indications for additional screw fixation14,23,24 (Resources 6, 7, and 8)
Screw Placement Considerations
A safe quadrant for screw placement is defined by two lines from the anterior superior iliac
spine through the center of the acetabulum and posteriorly by a line from the sciatic notch to
the center of the acetabulum25 (Resource 9)
In general, screws placed through posterosuperior and posteroinferior quadrants are safe and
do not emerge outside the pelvis.

Screw Placement Considerations
Inadvertent screw placement may cause neurovascular injury. A relatively retroverted
and vertically placed cup poses an increased risk for neurovascular injury. An
appropriately anteverted and abducted cup may minimize the risk of injury. In general,
screws aimed anterior to the sciatic notch are safe in native host bone in the ilium. In
general, screws placed through posterosuperior and posteroinferior quadrants are safe
and do not emerge outside the pelvis.26 In the posterosuperior quadrant, screws larger
than 25 mm often are placed in dense host bone for optimal screw fixation. Screws in
the posterosuperior quadrant usually do not need to be longer than 35 mm. Bicortical
fixation usually is unnecessary. Bicortical fixation is contraindicated in patients being
treated with anticoagulants because retroperitoneal hematoma and bone resorption
have been reported. During screw preparation, the sciatic nerve is protected by a finger
along the sciatic notch to prevent aberrant drill or screw penetration. In the
posteroinferior quadrant, screws should not be longer than 25 mm. The external iliac
vein and the iliac artery are at greatest risk with anterosuperior screws. The
neurovascular structures are located within 7 mm of the anterior column at the anterior
superior iliac spine and within 4 mm of the acetabular dome. The external iliac artery is
within 10 mm at the anterior superior iliac spine and within 7 mm of the acetabular

Complications
Inadvertent screw placement may cause neurovascular injury.

Complications
The most common injuries are those to the external iliac artery, femoral artery, and
external iliac vein27 (Figure 2).
Vascular injury identification is critical to expedite repair via vascular surgery. Visceral
injuries occur with inadvertent screw placement beyond the medial wall into the
retroperitoneum.
